blocks.x: JAZZ ORAL HISTORY PROJECT
Interview with Sammy Price by Dan Morgenstern
Institute of Jazz Studies
January 21, 1980
SAMMY PRICE
You were born in Honey Grove, Texas?
Yeah, I was born in Honey Grove, Texas. That's a little - small town in the eastern part of Texas.
What was the nearest big place?

Greenville...Paris...you know, in the eastern area you had Greenville, Paris and, if you went far enough, you'd go to Denison, up on the Red River Valley. I mean, the Red River... north of Honey Grove.
What was the musical environment there...I mean, what was the first music you heard...at home, or...?

I came from a line of religious preachers and gospel singers. Quite naturally, the first songs I heard would be... well, the lullabies, of course, but then, right off the bat we started going to church, so we heard many of the gospel songs, and the church songs, and hymns and things of that sort. And occasionally, when we were big enough, go and go and we used to/visit...not inside the church, but, outside, and listen to the Church of God and Christ singing, they played you know, with tambourines and a peculiar thing/called, you know, the triangle. You know what a triangle is? They played the triangle in the church and...there were very few pianos, of course--some broken-down organs, and many of the songs were a capella, with sometimes a preacher leading, or, you know, that kind of thing, where
the preacher would start a song; he would say the words, and the members would repeat after him, and then build up into a climax / (laughter) like Henry Red Allen'
Did you say you have brothers and sisters?

I had one brother. His name was Robert. He was two years older than I was, and we were known throughout Texas as the Price Boys. Not like the Daltons, or the Jesse James Boys; we were the Price Boys, and we were quite well known at first because/my father was a baker, you know, in Waco, and a lot of people used to come to him because he used to sell bread in our home, you see...a lot of people used to come. Then my grandfather, was a well-known A.M.E. minister, going from town to town each year, to build a new church. You see, in the south, with conditions as they were, church people...ministers, I'd say, were the liaison between the white man and the natives. Quite naturally, they had to have someone, and this minister was usually the liaison person. And...but my grandfather had fourteen kids, boys and girls, and then he had all these grandkids, naturally, and he used to go from town to town each year, when they had the quarterly Conference, which was a meeting of the various flocks; their leaders would come together, and then there was a presiding elder and a bishop, and they would determine where the assignments would be. Well, in ten years, my grandfather had an assignment in ten different cities. And he wondered why. But what my grandfather used to do was go

into a town where the conditions were deplorable and inadequate facilities for the church/ meeting; he'd take his fourteen kids and build a new church. Quite naturally that everybody wanted. So finally he asked the presiding elder why it is that he was always moved. "Well (said the elder), can't you see the handwriting on the wall? When you go into a church, and go into a new city and build a church/ everybody want you." So that was the history of doing quite a bit of traveling on his part for the first ten years of my life.
And then you moved to Dallas?

No, from Greenville we moved to Waco. We thought Waco was... about you know...talking/ Waco was like going to Heaven. Now, I'll tell you something, Danny, and this is a fact. Do you know that I was thirty years of age, and I was getting around in fast circles, before I realized that Jerusalem was not in Heaven. I was thirty years of age, and a friend of mine, Arthur Reid, who was a public speaker here in New York City, called it to my attention, that the church used Land to teach; if to go into Beulah/ you would have to cross the River of Jordan, and to cross the River of Jordan, you're going to go to Jerusalem, and when you get to Jerusalem, you're going to walk into Jerusalem just like John, and we couldn't separate this then...I really...it was a confusing story, but nobody ever bothered to explain it to us, so we lived with that. And I was almost thirty before I knew

that if I wanted to go to Jerusalem, I would have to buy thing a ticket to Jerusalem. And, it's a funny/ when you say that, you know...that's there's a lot of people that thought to go to Jerusalem, you know,........to cross the River Jordan, you have to go to Heaven. But then we... when I was four...we moved to Dallas, to Waco. And this is when we moved into a little subdivision of Waco, called West Station. West Station was maybe four or five miles out of the city. And, when the time came for us to make this big leap to the big, monstrous city, you know, we were up at four o'clock in the morning...the train came, and then we got on and we went to Waco. My father had a job as a baker in one of the local bakery shops, a big one, so we moved to Waco, and then they moved to West Station, and this is when life really started to begin for us.
Up to that point, you hadn't had any musical instruction or anything?

I hadn't had any musical instructions until shortly there- I'll tell you, after, I hadn't reached that point,/but up 'til that time I had just listened, and I'd hear these gospel songs... very religious...well, I mean when I say very religious, I mean we went to church on Sundays. Sunday morning we had Sunday School, then the main service, then in the afternoon they would have some special singers coming, and after the singers, they would have the night service.

So you see that meant that you had a lot of time to hear a lot of singing and a majority of the ceremonies were songs. Dan , you know, I'm surprised today to hear people talk about how many great piano players there were during that period. I didn't see that many pianos. They had organs. There were small organs that you played with your foot, the tambourine, and the triangle. Those were the instruments that I saw. The violin, that was for white folks, and all that trumpet, and all that business. We had a few, but they were so rare, that it wasn't even worth even mentioning.
No marching bands...?

Very few marching bands. There were very few marching bands. I don't remember...well, before I left Waco, they had marching bands, but around 1912, '13, there were very few marching bands. You know, and there was this war hysteria, you know what I mean, and it was just before World War I when in 1914 you had the conflict in Europe. Very few marching bands. People marched, but they didn't march with bands. You didn't have that many/ instrumentalists let's face it. said I'd I'd like to see that...sometimes I/ like to go to Wurlitzer's and look in the archives and see how many pianos did they sell in various regions, and I'd bet it would be alarming, that you'd have very few. You know, people

start talking about who did this and who did that, but back in those days if Eubie Blake played, he was a rarity. And the piano wasn't in tune. Because they didn't have any piano tuners you know, that care, you played in just a dive, a juke joing, backwood, you know, that was the ind of thing, so you had very few instruments, and when I hear these guys talking about in Bunk Johnson did this and Bunk Johnson did that. It's possible that he did it, but he was a rare case.
But we'll get to that a little later on...
Yeah, yeah...
So how did you come to play at the theater?

Well, what happened was, when I was about seven, there was a man that played a cornet, named Professor Cobb, a rarity. And I asked my mother if I could take lessons with Professor Cobb, and she said yes. And Professor Cobb taught me for two weeks, 25 cents a lesson. And then he talked to my mother and he said, "Mrs. Price, your son ain't got it. He just don't have it. He don't understand what it's all about." And she said, "Well, do you think that he can learn?" He said, "He can never learn. He has no conception of music and no conception of rhythm and no conception of tonal qualities, so that's that. So just save your 25 cents." And this sort of, you know, cooled me down for a while. But when I was seven or eight, then you started having drummers, and lodges and various

organizations would have...then they started developing bands where that you had a bass drummer that played the bass. They didn't have all these contraptions...all this new stuff. The guy had a cymbal on the top of the bass and he played a mallet. He played the bass drum with a mallet. And then you had a man playing the snare drum. But you know what I'm thinking...perhaps these things were not accessible to black communities so this may be a reason why I wouldn't know, I would not be exposed to it. If it's in a white theater you just pass by and see, Tom Thumb or some band or something, but it would not mean anything to me because of the fact that I didn't ever have an opportunity to see it, you know, to get inside that theater and to really get close up to the drummer, because they didn't allow blacks in many of those places.
Do you want to say anything about traveling shows?

Now what happened about the traveling shows, when I was about eight, in Waco, which we were still living in Waco, we used to have carnivals and they would have road shows and minstrels and things like that. But a kid seven years of age is not going to have an opportunity to learn... when I say to learn, I think to learn something about music, about dancing, you got to be exposed to it. You got to be up close to it. And we didn't have that opportunity. Later on we did, but this, you see, was about

the turn of the century; this was, when I say about the turn of the century, about 1914, when you had the war in Europe, and I used to sit around; then you started having marching bands--you know, drums and, you know, , and some blacks going into the army and some guy that probably could play the drums was a drummer, and then you had a trumpet player who could probably play that music of that age, you know, marching bands, you see. But then, shortly thereafter, I used to hear the men from Europe...you know, I used to sit around shining shoes in a shining parlor, and hear the soldiers that were being trained in America to be pilots and in other kinds of warfare and they used to just fascinate me with all these stories about London...London, you know!..but I didn't know where in the hell London was, you see. And then there were some strange things that we had there, that you wouldn't believe. You know, I used to believe when I was young that when it rained in Waco that it rained all over the world. I didn't have any idea that it rained in Waco and not rain in the next county. I thought that when it rained in Waco that was it, it was raining all over the world. These are unfortunate things, regrettably so, but then this is a fact. 'Cause I just think when it rain, when it thunder, when it thundered here it thundered in New York, Washington,Cleveland...although I didn't know these towns, because I hadn't been

exposed to them. But shortly thereafter I asked my mother if I could go up and meet Ella B. Moore. Now, Ella B. Moore and Chinch Moore had a show they used to bring to the Cotton Palace in Waco--that was like a big festival they'd have, maybe for nineteen days...they'd have a big fair and they'd have a rodeo...but they always would have a colored show. And they had these people who worked on minstrels and worked on carnivals and worked on road shows. They always had some of them at these shows.

So I went up and I asked Ella B. Moore where she was from and she said, Dallas. Well, Dallas was 99 miles north of Waco. And she asked me my name, and she said, "You know, I'm going to call you Willie." I told her my name was Sammy. She said, "I'm going to call you Willie because I like you." And I promised her that someday I would make that big trip from Waco, you know, 99 miles north to see her. And she says, "Well, okay." They had a theater, a little theater in Waco called the Park Theater. Used to have vaudeville shows when they could get, You know, acts. So, that was my first introduction to a person on the stage. (Telephone interruption.) Then I met Daybreak Nelson./ Where were we?
You were talking about little theater where they...
Oh, the Gaiety Theater. So, finally my mother decided... Well, the Park Theater. The Gaiety Theater was in Waco and from time to time they had had road shows coming in.

And I had an opportunity to see Daybreak Nelson, who was a comedian, and some dancers and some singers... early singers of that period. Finally the time came that my mother decided to move to Dallas. She went ahead and got a little house for us and in 1918 we moved to Dallas. Well, I got right off the Inter-Urban and went straight to the Park Theater to find Ella B. Moore. Now I didn't have any idea that Mrs. Moore would have anything to do, Danny, with my playing music. You know, because in those days you were not sure...I didn't know whether I wanted to be a dancer...I couldn't make up my mind...the guy said I couldn't play...he had me paranoid 'cause he said that I couldn't understand anything about music and don't even...you know, so that was a thing that was not discussed in my household. So, one day I was walking up the street. I heard a player piano--by this time now they were in vogue, and popular and-with people had a few dollars, you know, I guess you could buy it now and pay for it later. My brother and I passed this lady's house, and she said, "You boys want to make some money?" My brother said, "No way." you know, he wanted to stay away from work as far as he could. I asked the lady, "Doing what?" She said, "you know, helping me clean the house and raking the leaves and so forth." I said. "I'll take the job if you'll

let me practice on your piano." Just like that. Now, that was my introduction...those were the first words spoken, you know, about the piano. She says, "Okay, some Saturday morning." And I came Saturday morning and I worked hard and finally the time came for me to go into this lady's parlor and sit down at the piano. Well, what I did was to play the piano roll and watch where the notes went down and then sequels like that, and I learned how to play a song called, "My Isle of Golden Dreams." That's how I learned it. And that was her favorite song. And I wore that song out, you know what I mean, I played it everywhere I'd go, you know, in whatever key if they did have a piano--there were two or three people in my neighborhood--Martha Turner & Dave Allen had pianos, see, and I used to go and play that and then I would play it the way [it was] originally and I'd play with a lot of rhythm, you know what I mean, and then just fool around and just improvise and, you know, that was my first introduction to the piano.
So you really taught yourself...

Yeah...well later by Mrs. Pittman,, Booker T. Washington's daughter. Later. But my first introduction to the piano was that lady asking me if I wanted to do some work for her. And I said yes. I don't know how that came out of my mouth, "Yes, I will, if you'll

let me play the piano." And then from that, I became big and bold. In 1923 the Charleston dance came out. And I became like an exceptional Charleston dancer. Now doing these dances, Danny, did one thing for me. It taught me to have confidence before an audience.
You were saying that dancing in front of people gave you confidence.

Yeah. Yeah, that's...we call it...I hear people call it stage fright, stage presence, you know, being before an audience, being afraid, being nervous, forgetting...if you sing, forget the words or if you're a dancer forgetting part of the routine, or a musician...well, that dancing did quite a bit for me. And it furthered my musical career. Because (our tendency with that?) I was studying with Mrs. Pittman by then.
She was a music teacher?

She was a music teacher, yes. She was a school teacher and music, she taught music. So what I did was to study with her, you know, and then I would dance, you know, and the opportunity came to join Alphonso. Mrs. Pittman said to me when she first heard me touch the piano, you know, she wanted to see how I knew and how I could play little things. She said, "Sammy, you have an exceptional knowledge of the instrument. You know, and a good feeling. I don't know if you'll ever become a great reading musician, but you can share your
feeling with other musicians who are trained." That was exactly what she said to me, and I thought that was a pretty good compliment.
Yeah, but that's kind of unusual, because at that time music teachers were, you know...

Was real strict, you know, the eighth note, hit your hand...why didn't you see that accidental, that's an eighth note, that's a B-flat, and so forth. But she said that to me. And then I paid attention to that. But Bud Goldberg, who was the manager of Alphonso Trent's orchestra, came up to a dance in the black community with Trent. And he saw me out on the floor dancing, and everybody was crowded around me, you know, when you're a crowd-seeker, you know, and he said to Trent, "Why don't we take that dancer and let him dance with the band, you know, when they play the Adolphus Hotel or some big places, you know, white people they want to see a black kid dancing." And I could really do the Charleston. The Charleston had become a rage across America and really, if you could do the Charleston you were it in those days, and do it well. So they decided that I would go like to Mineral Wells or Austin or Houston or wherever they'd go. And they didn't allow...I could go in with the band and sit behind the piano until the time come for me to come out and do my Charleston. The band would pay

me and then I'd get a lot of tips. So this is how I really broke into like what I call the big time. But one of the things that happened was, that sitting behind that piano for three or four hours, I had an opportunity to really listen at changes--hearing a guy play a different kind of thing, or hear now the trumpets coming in, or the piano would be playing--this is a piano solo or clarinet solo, so I had an opportunity during the period that I was with Trent to know these things, which didn't hurt.
Was Trent the piano player?

Yeah, Alphonso was the piano player. He liked me and he used to...then I used to start bugging him to show me things. Whenever we would go...say if we were playing the Adolphus Hotel, we may arrive at the place an hour before, you understand, and he may be practicing like, learning a new song or something. I could sit in on the rehearsals. I began to hear, you know, "That's a B-flat...tune your horn," and that business. So I had an opportunity to learn something about music and about the piano and about how to play soft, and tonal quality and, you know, various rhythms and that thing. That really started me then...... you couldn't stop me. Then I got a job...a man heard...by this time there was some talk that, "Sam Price is dancing with the Alphonso Trent Band," and,

"Sam Price has learned...man, he's playing the piano," and this, that and the other. You know, I could play the Charleston, you know I could play 'My Isle of Golden Dreams' the "Charleston," or whatever there it was, I'd play these things. So finally this man came to me and said, he wanted me to come to Athens, Texas, to play for a dance. He'd pay me five dollars a night for a Saturday and Sunday. And I could...Christmas was on Monday, so I had an opportunity to go and play for him and come back and be home in time for Christmas. So that was the first professional job I said that I had. Just the piano...it was out of tune...and you know what I mean. But before that I had so much nerve that a guy came looking for a piano player to play for a man that wanted somebody to play for him, so I said, 'I play the piano, so the guy took me up to this club, big club, and this guy was sitting there with a bottle of whiskey and he said, "play me some music!"' And I played 'My Isle of Golden Dreams$ ." Then he said, 'okay, now, play me some blues. I played 'My Isle of Golden Dream$' He says, "Okay, play me something with the Charleston. I played, 'My Isle .." He told me, "Get the hell out of here," and he gave me five dollars. That was the first...(laughter). So now we are up to that first job.

PRICE: 5.
DM: 25...
PRICE: 1925. Then I by this time was very, very close to Ella B. Moore. Well, I could dance and this gave me the opportunity--she had a little amateur show of kids; they were pretty good, though, you know, do little drama things and chorus girls and, you know--so in 1925 she said to me, "Willie, you know I think you're going to be a musician." Right then I says, "Why?" She says, "I hear you always fooling around." Wherever I saw a piano--they were so rare there--that wherever I saw one I ran right to it, you know, so she says, "I hear you always fooling around my piano. How would you like to go out this summer on a little road show. So what happened--show people used to wear shoes without laces, you know, they were...you know, you take a shoe horn and put the shoe on, but it was--just like these shoes that I have now--they have this thing on it, but it was no top, you know, they had a top but there wasn't anything on it. So the first thing I did when she said that was to go buy me a pair of those shoes like the road shows. And I'd stand around the theater when, say, Cow Cow Davenport came to town and Jesse Crump, who was my favorite, who played for Ida Cox. When Jesse came to town I would always...I would be

at the theater when they come and I would stay until they left. I watched everything and tried to just be a professional person in that way. And then, actually I was improving on my piano playing. And people would let me play now that...around at the house-rent parties I was, you know, popular. Very popular. That was in 1925, and I went up...we went up to Okmulgee, Oklahoma. This is where I first met Oscar Pettiford.
Is he the bass player ?
Right.
He was a kid.
They had a family...

They had a family band, yeah. A family band in Okmulgee, Oklahoma. And that's when I first saw him. And then I met Walter Page. Walter Page and Willie Lewis had the Blue Devils and they had a good band. Hot Lips Page later joined them in Tulsa. And then I just became ......., but I was playing more and more... not for money. I used to just play and give the money to the other person. If they would say, 'it's bad and we want you to play tonight, will you help us out?' 'Yeah.' They'd have seven, eight musicians...didn't get much money anyway. And I could gamble--you know what I mean--I knew all those things, you know, how to gamble...and I could go some place and dance and get extra money. So I would go and play with the

band. And you know, Budd Johnson and Buster Smith, Dad Minor—I don't know if you know who Dad Minor is, he's a trombone player ...Dan Minor and John R. Davis and Willie Owens...these were all local lights, but they were well known. Like you had another segment in Dallas, like Troy Floyd and Benny Long and people like that who went with Trent, and Benno Kennedy and these musicians...
Benno Kennedy was a trumpet player?

Oh, was he a trumpet player! He was fantastic. Benno was really nice. He played with Trent. I think he came from Wichita Falls. That's the same place that Herschel Evans came from. And...I think that playing music, Dan, can become contagious and then, if you have any insight or any...this damn guy that said that I didn't know anything about music, he's crazy. Because he didn't realize that I have this innate feeling for this stuff, you know. And that moment that the woman asked me to do--you know what I mean--to do that work, then I think that's when it was born; I just decided to let it break out--you know what I mean--and this is it, you know what I mean. What do you mean telling me that I can't...that I don't have no...I think that anybody can learn some things. For example, they say the white musicians can't play, but I don't want anybody telling me Gene Krupa wasn't a good musician. I don't want

them telling me that Benny Goodman, no matter if he was classically trained...he was a good musician. But I think because we think in the tradition of heritage, of that black heritage, that may be the thing that people have not been able to unscramble. And the writers need to determine what we're talking about. See we're talking about here...when we speak of jazz, then we speak of a thing that's a black thing. Now, that don't mean that it has to necessarily remain that. But then we think that there should be those original roots.
Speaking of that, when did you first hear the blues?

Oh, the first time I heard the blues was in Waco. A man had been...well the blues...in 1915, a black man had been lynched in a town called Robertsonville. I didn't pay any attention to the blues that much...this guy...because blues were considered vulgar and you couldn't sing it at home--sometime your father run you away from home, you had to leave home if you sang, you know, "Goin' Down to the River, Take a Rocking Chair." Well now, what had happened was...the song was...he had a parody. The parody was, "I never have and I never will/ Pick no more cotton in Robertsonville/ Tell me how long will I have to wait?/ Can I get you now or must I hesitate?" And that was the "How Long Blues." Right? But Blind Lemon Jefferson in 1915-16, in that

time,used to come to Waco and pick his big guitar and sing "Going Down to the River, Take a Rocking Chair/ The Blues overtake Me, Going to Rock Away From Here." And sang various blues that they make up. You know, in the black community, if a guy...if his woman left him to go up to [the] country, you know, he'd compose a song. Got a new pair of shoes, if he went to prison for ten years, they would create songs based on whatever the incident of the evening was. ....How are you running on?
It's still going.
Yeah. And...but Blind Lemon Jefferson was the first blues singer that I paid attention to. And do you know that I had something to do with him making records? Years later? Did you know that?
Yeah, I heard something, about that.

All right. J.Mayo Williams was with the company. And he came down to Dallas. And a man named R. T. Ashford had a record shop and he used to get talent. He had a woman named Hattie Burl&son and Victoria Spivay and those people. And I went to him and I said, "You know, Mr. Ashford, Blind Lemon Jefferson I think will sound good on records." And he said, "Mmmmmh." And he never indicated to me that, you know, that he would negotiate. So he got together with the record company and that's how Blind Lemon Jefferson made his first
record. And I didn't get anything for it. Boy, I can certainly reminisce! (Laughter).

I can think that I had something to do with it because...and then they started to have Corley Waters play the mandolin, and Texas Alexander, who was a blues singer (I trained him), he never could...he didn't have...now there's a guy that didn't know anything, that the fellow--- the music teacher said that I would never...Texas Alexander had no concep...he just could carry a melody in the middle part. But he didn't know when to end and when to stop or anything. And then I helped him quite a bit.
Blind Lemon Jefferson I think was almost the first of that kind of a singer which we now call a Country Blues...
Right.
They hadn't recorded much...
Right, they hadn't done very much of that. 'Cause, well, during those days you had Bessie Smith, Ida Cox...
Ma Rainey...

Yeah, Ma Rainey and Bert Williams. Incidentally.....let me tell you a story. One time my mother...Mamie Smith had made "The Crazy Blues." It was a very, very popular thing. So they said...wanted me to go and buy "The Crazy Blues." Now, instead of my going to the black store to buy it, I went to the white store to buy it. And I asked for "The Crazy Blues." The guy gave me

this "Crazy Blues" in a package and I went home and they said, "now if you break this I'm not going to exchange it." you know. So I walked very carefully and then I got home and they had a Gramophone, and my mother wound this thing up and put a needle in and put this "Crazy Blues" on and they thought that they were going to hear Mamie Smith and out came Bert Williams singing "The Crazy Blues." (Laughter)
Was the record store of the Ashford, was that in the black neighborhood?

Yeah, it was on the Central Track. And it was...actually, I don't think he could make it just selling records, do you understand? So he had a shoeshine parlor-- sold shoelaces and things. And he had about seven guys that shined shoes. And I used to shine shoes there because the people wanted the Charleston King to shine their shoes. So you see, all through life I've always tried to figure how to stay one step ahead of the sheriff. (Laughter)

Well those kinds of record stores were still around down South when I was in the army. I was stationed in Georgia--Columbus, Georgia they had those kinds of stores, too. In the front there was a shoeshine parlor and then they'd sell some hushpuppies and...
Right, right...
And then in back they had the records.....
Right, right. Shoeshining was a real, real lucrative item for blacks because it was one thing that you could make some money and very little investment.
So when did you...when you had your first job and you did go out and this was still around Texas, were you still living at home, basically?

Yeah, I always lived at home. I never lived away from home in Dallas, in Texas. I always lived at home. Because I was taught and trained to be very, very faithful and respectful. I'm over-respectful now to people. When I say, 'Yes, ma'am' and 'no, ma'am,' people think I'm crazy. It's not that, it's just that I was taught that way. I remember one time...people used to see us, you know, the Price boys, and they would say, 'These nice boys and this little old colored lady.' So one time we went to visit a friend on a streetcar...had to go to another section of the city and when we got to the other section of the city, coming back we got on the streetcar. The streetcar would stop and you would have to get on the streetcar in the front, pay your fare, and then walk the left of the streetcar to the back of the streetcar. So my brother, mother and myself did that and there were some kids from Baylor University--football players--picked a fight with us. Well, they were sitting in the white section and we had to walk through, and then they tripped us and punched

my mother. Well, my mother was like, when you say "fight," she...it was all right with her, you know what I mean...and then we were right with her and we beat the hell out of all those football players on that streetcar. We jumped up and there was a sign-- they had signs--there was a sign setting at an angle, "Colored" on one side, "White" on the other. I jumped up and got that sign, boy, and I was beating guys... I think that they thought it would be just a little melee where "These niggers are going to run," and all that. But boy, we fought 'em, and the guy drove that streetcar fast as he could right down to the city hall. And do you know they let those people that beat us up, that jumped on us, they let them get away. (End of Side 1)
When did you actually go out, you know, leave home, and...

And really go far away? In 1927 Leonard Reed, who was a dancer, who used to be very, very close to Joe Louis, was in Dallas with his wife. We were naturally at the Ella B. Moore Theater. A show came to town, a traveling show in the TOBA. You know about...you know...well, the TOBA was a circuit similar to the Orpheum Time and various white routes that stars traveled. And he was quite unusual, and he used to go around various sections of the country and play in piano appearances with colleges, you know, and competitions. So that's as nearly as I can recall to my first meeting with him was that he was in that category. Now there's a professional performer. So that's ......... first knew him. But really to know him, was in Chicago when Lovey Taylor told Earl Hines there was a kid in the house that could play the piano and he play "Tiger Rag," you know, like a shotgun. I mean that...I've never seen an expression...well, I saw one other expression on Earl Hines' face, you know what I mean, it was like a thing of amazement. That was when we were going to Europe in 1948 with Louis Armstrong--he was with Louis, you know--and there were several bands going for that International Festival in Nice and Earl Hines and Jack Teagarden and Sid Catlett and Barney Bigard and Arvell Shaw and Velma Middleton, Louis, and...who was playing trombone... in that band?
Teagarden.
Jack Teagarden, yeah. Jack was amazing. Jack use to go into a town and...he had a very, very sensitive

ear about tone, you see, and true tone. Jack would go into a town and if there was just one note off on that piano he'd take off his clothes and tune the piano. But we were out at--I think it was LaGuardia... I don't think Kennedy was in existence at that time and...Kennedy wasn't in existence at that time, and all the airports were just being built and they just had one shed. I can never forget the time that, you know, when we got up to playing with Louis and the Mayers and Baby Dodds, Pops Foster and Jimmy Archey and Henry Goodwin and we got off in...it was very, very cold in Paris during the time of the festival. And no heat and no place indoors, and when you got off that plane and we walked around for an hour just for the newspapers to make shots.. and TV and so forth. But, speaking of Earl Hines, when we got on the plane in New York, at LaGuardia Airport, the exhaust had a fire. you know. like...I don't know what the hell it was. but this fire came out of this exhaust. you know. and you could see it. And Earl Hines was frozen from LaGuardia to Orly Airport just watching that fire. He thought the plane was on fire. (Laughter) But we had a big laugh about that.
Was that your first time in Europe?
Yep. 1948. It was very, very interesting. We were supposed to land in...at....what the hell were we

supposed to do, we were supposed to land in Nice. But then they couldn't land in Nice because of the conditions and we had to go all the way back to Orly Airport in Paris and we landed in Paris. Panassié was having a fit. Well actually, do you know that I went to Europe that year by accident. Again, you see. So perhaps fate has played a role with me on many evenings in my life and many points in my life, just as the lady saying to me, "Do you want to do some work?" Willie "the Lion" Smith was slated to go to Europe and Willie didn't go. And Mayers asked me to come. He didn't let Panassié know because days of communication were, you know what I mean, you write a letter today and you get an answer next...whatever you got the answer it would be too late to do whatever you wanted to do. So they just simply switched Willie "the Lion's" ticket over to me and I went in his stead. And it really created a furor...and Johnny (Zimmer?) later told me, and then I think they wrote about how confusing it was, that they were looking for Willie "the Lion" Smith and when they called on the telephone they were trying to determine who the replacement for Willie "the Lion" Smith was and Panssié was, you know, yelling and the producer was yelling, and they said, "Pappy Drake----Pappy Rice".....they didn't know what name it was. that they (Laughter.) So finally it dawned on Hugues, were saying
"Sammy Price." He says, "Merveilleux Mayers" , you know, 'he's so marvelous with his ideas.' So, and that's how I happened to get to Europe..that first time.

We left off...I think, you know, we'd been talking about a lot of things so we got away from the chronology, but we didn't talk about...I guess you went to Chicago, that was one place where you spent some time...

Yeah...well, I spent almost a year in Chicago. What had happened was, when I left the TOBA after the conclusion of that ill-fated tour, we went to Atlanta and...well, I've yet to tell you how I got my first wife, you know...we ll pick up there.

We left Memphis and went to Virginia. I'm not saying that that's the manner in which it was done or whether that's the time, but . We went to Danville, Virginia, and we had this show and a man by the name of Boisse DeLegge had , came into town at the same time we were there. So people used to just try to steal...not steal...but entice people from one show to the other. So the show that we were on needed three more people to go...well, four people...to go into Danville, Virginia. So we...there was a guy named Herbert Hubert, the guy that wrote "I'm Falling for You," and his wife and the two dancers--he had a singing group and dancing group. So we met at this restaurant and we were talking and, you know, people didn't get any money...you didn't get any money...they just didn't pay you 'cause they didn't have it. If they didn't
have it they didn't give it to you. So we asked Joe Hubert to come and join our show and leave Boisse DeLegge and come with Happy Donovan and Travis Tucker. He said all right, he'd do it.

Well, somehow Boisse DeLegge found out that Joe was going to leave the show. So Joe was trying to hide around to keep him from catching up with him. So finally he caught up with Joe and Boise was, you know, from New Orleans, and with a hot temper, and so he belted Joe one right in the eye. Well, Joe was ready to stay with the show, you know but naturally ...people agitating, he said, 'Well, you haven't paid me for the last eight weeks,' and that was the only way he could get away from the show, because the guy knew he hadn't paid him. So that's how he got away from the show.

So we went to Danville, Virginia, and in this hotel... if well, usually the shows...there were five chorus girls that were single, and there were five men that were single, before the evening was over you had five marriages, you know. Not shotgun, but... (laughter)...you know, performed by the manager. That was because he would save the cost of five rooms, you know, an economic solution. That's so if you got married, or if you lived in common law, just sleeping with a person in a room, then that was just one room, see, so instead of having to rent ten rooms, you only had to rent five.
So we were in this hotel in Danville, Virginia. The police raided the hotel and said, 'Everybody out in the hallway.' Well, five doors opened and here are ten people. The man said,

"Now, if this is your wife, I want to see the marriage license. And if it's not your wife, you're going to jail." Well, when I got down to the jail (laughter) the man...the manager of the show...put up a bond and we went...we had to leave Virginia because I was not 21...had to leave Virginia and go to North Carolina, get married, and then bring that license back to Virginia and present it to the man, and whatever bond it was... fifty, a hundred, two hundred dollars, you's get your money back.

Well, what I should have done, when they let me out of jail, I should have kept running fast as I could, but I was going to be really...you know, I took the thing seriously. I'll get married and have a home, you know, and we'll save money... now, how could you do any of these things with the man not paying you? You were lucky if you got a room and some food, and that's all you got. But one of the things that we got on the TOBA 'Dan, was that--almost like a letter of understanding-- that you respect each other, and very rarely did you ever hear mis- of misuse of trust by any of those persons, 'cause that was a thing that you were really taught, and it was really good.

Now, we went on when we got married and went to Atlanta, went to Norfolk. Well, my wife ran away. She said, "I can't take this. No food..." I tell her, "Come back, I'll make a better home," you know...so then we finally ended up in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And when we ended up in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, this is when the show broke up.

Now, I knew...I knew how to live...I knew, just like I say, I knew women and I knew that a woman would be nice to you, 'specially if she's older than you, or something like that. And I had to use that. And there were five guys with us and then they looked at me like I was a father, you know, I was the champion of the band... and I'd go out and get money and food and tailor shop and...we were living pretty good in Pittsburgh.

And finally one day my wife, who was very, very jealous, asked me, "Where are you getting this money?" And I told her that I was getting it from Lena Horne's father, Teddy Horne, who lived in Pittsburgh. She followed me one night to this woman's house and she was yellin' all over the place, she was going to kill the woman and kill me and kill herself and all that. We ended up no food, you know, back (laughter)...we ended up back where we started from, you know what I mean, on zero.

Well, a show came through, and as I said, they always need people. So we got on the show and went from Pittsburgh to Washington and then in Washington that show broke up. Then we got on another show and went from Washington to Baltimore and back. We just...nothing was consistent, nothing was real, you know, it was...I tried one time to become a comedian in Washington. So they said, "Yeah, we need a comedian"...that's why they needed that other person...more than one person. So I got on the show in Washington and the man said, "Well, you're

a comedian," and he gave me my lines, you know, and I looked real stupid. I walked out on the stage and I was supposed to say, "Are you there?" and the woman is supposed to answer to that, "Yes, you're there, you'd better stay there, you're a big, black bear," just like that. You know, I couldn't remember those words! I got fired from that.

So finally we decided to take a show and go back, you know, backtrack to Louisville and all those places that we played. So we ended up in 1928 at Christmas back in Dallas. And was I glad to get a good dinner. Turkey, and all that business.

Well, now we're coming to 1929. I decided after a while that the traveling fever...well, you know...was in my blood. It's pretty rugged to live in like the South, or some small town after you've experienced St. Louis and Washington and Louisville and all those towns, you know, and fast towns and you seen Ida Cox and Lovey Taylor and Trixie Smith and Mamie Smith and this...the feeling that I got of being somebody more important than just going over to some local dance hall and hear some guy play, hear somebody sing that are really amateurs. I just felt that I was above that. A show came to Dallas. I went to Tulsa; from Tulsa to Oklahoma City and from Oklahoma City to Kansas City. And I stayed in Kansas City from '29 to '32. And in 1932...this is in Kansas City when Count Basie was there and it meant nothing to see...[phone rings]
You were talking about when Count Basie was in Kansas City...

Well, we get to Kansas City...Kansas City to me at that point was the highlight. It wasn't the climax, but just the highlight...well, I don't guess it was the highlight, but it was such an exciting city, where that...at six o'clock you 'O have Julia Lee, George Lee, Andy Kirk, Mary Lou Williams, Hot Lips Page, Willie Mack Washington who was the first drummer with Bennie Moten, Jo Jones...well, I don't think Jo was around in the beginning. And then you'd have Dan Miner and Budd Johnson and Keg Johnson, Booker Pittman, Count Basie, Buster Moten, Buster Smith, Hot Lips Page, Walter Page, all of the musicians that...and Ben Webster...all of the musicians that you had known over the years and you had picked them as possibly going to the top of the heap, WERE in Kansas City. And then you had like Louis coming to town and you had Don Redman, McKinney's Cotton Pickers, you know, all of the leading attractions.

This was fascinating to me. And then I was...I called myself half-slick, you know what I mean. I was good friends with Ellis Burton, who was the owner of the Yellow Front Cafe, and Piney Brown...(unintelligible).. Piney Brown and--Big Piney had gone to Chicago to live, but Little Piney was there--and Felix Payne, who was another patron of jazz musicians. And Big Joe Turner, Jimmy Rushing. And this to me was just so fascinating and amazing, that I just couldn't...I couldn't really get it in my mind that here I am, Sammy Price, who the lady asked did I want to, you know, do
some work. And Sammy Price, who the music teacher said I would never play, I had no ideas. Flashbacks... [recording interruption]
We were still in Kansas City. You were saying how amazed you were that, you know, that you found yourself there...
With all that fast company?
Yeah.. Was Lester around then? In Kansas City?

Lester was there and was one of the most outstanding musicians and stylists that I've ever met. I don't ever remember having met a person that was as unique. And he was sort of like a cute man, you know, and he was a man, too, but he was cute. He was just a cute man...sweet, high, nice, polite, kind, but mean as hell. But all of the good parts always came out of him at all times. And...Lester Young. Who did I leave out that was...well, no...I said Buster Smith, didn't I?
Yes, yes...

Stuff Smith was there at one time, but not as much. Jimmy Mundy was there. We had a very, very famous pianist named Emil Williams, I don't know if you ever heard of him, and...it's amazing that Benno Kennedy didn't ever come to Kansas City during those days, those two or three years I was there. Let's see. Who else was there that...we're leaving somebody out.
Well, there were so many musicians...
Thamon Hayes, Pha Terrell, Tickle Toe...
Who was that?
He was a dancer. And...you know, strange as it seems...as it may seem to you, to many people...lay people, persons...
wherever there was a style of music played or a song created, did you know they created a dance to go along with it?

For example, you take like the Charleston. James P. wrote that song, "The Charleston." James P. should have become the richest...you're talking about Elvis Presley and those guys. The Charleston was well received all over the world. Now, why didn't James P. have thirty-five million dollars to divide like the Rolling Stones on somebody else's song? What happened? How did it happen? And you gotta remember, too, that we're speaking of music and style that...many of the songs that were written by the white musicians were played and became popular with the blacks, like "Lady Be Good." A lot of people thought that Count Basie wrote "Lady Be Good." You know who wrote "Lady Be Good," right? Do you know?
Gershwin.
Yeah, George. And you know, in other songs, in other compositions, in other...let's see, like "Ballin' the Jack." Chris...
Smith.

Chris Smith wrote "Ballin' the Jack." But there was a dance called "Ballin' the Jack." And then, on and on, and I can think of a series of songs, you know what I mean, and these songs had a dance to go along with it. So I think that the dancing and the music are so interrelated that you have...when you think of one you have to think of the other. Sometimes, maybe, the dancers...I think like in the case of the Charleston,
I think that the dance was out before the song. But it's amazing, though, how related they were to each other.

But, in Kansas City...I used the term "slick." I wasn't never slick, 'cause I never tried to fleece anybody, you know, or tried to sell the Brooklyn Bridge. I just would... my thing was with ladies. You know, I could make it with... you know what I mean. And really, when I come to think of it, I don't think they made too much of a contribution, I think it was just that confidence that they gave me, that made me...because I...long as I can remember, I've always worked. So I wasn't a pimp. I wasn't, you know, like, you know, had to have...live in somebody's house, or some woman had to keep me and come and bring my rent--I always worked. But I think that in my mind, I wanted to think that I was slick. Just like Eddie Barefield said, every time he ever played, that I showed up with a woman. Well, that's possibly true.

But in Kansas City I also have always been friendly with operators. You know, like people that owned the clubs and...they used to call people gangsters and all that. Well, I always was friendly with people.
Were they gangsters?

Mmmh...what is a gangster? I don't know what a gangster is, for want of a better word. I never saw any wrongdoing. I say this--I say that many of those persons that were accused of being gangsters, and all, were the ones that
had night clubs and places where musicians worked. So, if they were gangsters, they gave a lot of people work.
I guess Prohibition had something to do with that...were involved with selling liquor and it was illegal and you got........

Well, Prohibition was illegal ...well, everybody drank, so I mean, so they must have been getting the whiskey someplace. And perhaps...you know, writers create titles and pseudonyms and make references to certain things. And I know a lot of writers that wrote about Prohibition and were drunk, or they drank. And that was the purpose of going out, you know.

But the thing that I could never understand, Dan, is how in the hell that on weekends everybody'd go out and go into a club and the place'd be crowded and by word of mouth and, you know, and you'd have hundreds of people gathering and you'd have picnics and you didn't have...you couldn't put it in The Daily News, The Post wasn't available, The Village Voice wasn't available, the local papers printed once the week for blacks, and by the time that that came out on Friday or Saturday...but it was amazing how, that by word of mouth, these could become so famous, and so popular. And people people would know they're coming to town, and they would crowd out the dance halls. Well, when I say crowd out, you take a thousand people...a lot of people. And they'd have a dance hall with a thousand people in the place.

And fights galore, you know what I mean, and people fighting over the musicians and...and another segment of the people really loved them, really appreciated them and...I guess that's just the way society is structured. You're going to have these problems wherever you go.

Now I worked...I was a friend of Ellis Burton.. I had a problem with a woman and Ellis told...so, I'm told he said to a policemen that"It you say anything else to Sammy Price, don't come around me any more."

But anyway, I stayed my time out in Kansas City and I felt like, I guess, a disciple, that I was supposed to stay in a certain place, you know, until my time was out and then move on. In the meanwhile, I opened a restaurant in Topeka, Kansas. I was going with a girl named Valetta. I wrote a song...
Uh-huh, I've got that record.

You got that record? All right. Well, I wrote a song, "Valetta," and we had this restaurant, and when they had the crash--that was in '29--I had a lot of food on the stove, two or three cars and, you know, all of that, and no customers. And, just like I said, I didn't realize then, even 'til '29-- and I had traveled extensively and had read, of course...You know, in the beginning, and in the early twenties, you know, you didn't have radios like you have. Now you had these radios with earphones, like those earphones, and you had to touch a little--did you ever see that crystal set? And you touched that, and if you put it on the right spot, you could

hear it; but a lot of times--Earl Hines used to come from Chicago, you know, and we didn't have but one, one or two earphones, you know...we'd have one that you listen in and we'd all be trying to listen and sometimes somebody would touch that crystal and it would go off at the point, and you just couldn't hear it. When you'd come back when you'd get it again, he says, "Ladies and Gentlemen, Earl Hines will at 9.30 be on tomorrow night (laughter). But be that as it may, I think that we did pretty good with the conditions as they were.

But in 1933 I had a problem with a woman. So, I was so angry 'til I went out on the highway with my bags and this man that owned the Cherry Blossom came past...he was just going for a drive and he saw me and say, "where you going?" I say, "well, I'm going as far as you go." And do you know that I convinced that man, in Kansas City, to drive me to St. Louis at eight o'clock in the morning. I convinced that man, Dan, to drive me from St. Louis to 39th Street and South Parkway by the Grand Terrace. Now that's pretty good talking. And he did it and I guess he was glad, he was proud of it. Well, I guess he was so fascinated...I was telling him so many yarns about how great he was, and what he should do is to go to Chicago because there are a lot of chorus girls and pretty women and they'd come back to Kansas City with him, you know, without any hesitation whatsoever, and he went for it. He went for it, you know. And I was so embarassed...I went in one door in this
hotel next to the Grand Terrace...I went in one door and out the other.

I still remember how nice he was to me and I think this is what make me, you know, kind to people. If I see a person on the highway, if I can help, or...well, actually, I believe, though, that this kind of feeling that I have for helping people became more when my wife became ill, because after having a four year experience with my wife being ill from '74 to '78, then I had, you know, I created that soft spot in my heart... it really came to the fore. And I just really...I'm an old man myself, but I help old people across the street now that are probably younger than I am. Today no day will pass that I won't try to help a person. You know, I go out of my way to do it. In many instances I says, "How old are you, dear?" and she says, "61." I say, "Oh, gee, I got you by ten years." (laughter). But I say, somebody should be helping me across the street and here I am, the Good Samaritan.

But when I got to Chicago I knew a lot of people. Budd Johnson was there and other jazz musicians, you know, because they didn't all stay in the same place, they'd move around. So I knew Jesse Stone...oh, Jesse Stone was in Kansas City. Do you know about him?
He was a fine arranger, wasn't he?
And piano player. He was a good arranger, yeah. But Jesse was in Chicago and then, I knew a lot of other people. I knew a guy named Eddie Torrenti who was an old friend of
mine and then he was a friend of Valetta's. And then I met Jimmie Noone and then I met Earl Hines, Barney Bigard, Omer Simeon...Who was playing the drums for Earl Hines then? He lived in...ah....
Wally Bishop.
Walter Bishop. Yeah, I heard you. Was it Walter Bishop or was it....mmmh...
It was somebody before him...Earl's band...

I think it was Walter Bishop. But anyway you...and then I began to see where the Peking Restaurant was and seeing Louis and Teddy Wilson...In other words, I was like a person that had started in kindergarten with that man with that twenty-five cents and that woman saying this, and Mrs. Ella B. Moore saying this, and going on to those little road shows when I met Oscar Peterson.
Oh. I didn't tell you that when I was in Okmulgee, you know who I met? Count Basie, guy named Zeddie played trumpet, and one other , Kelly somebody. Somebody named Kelly. Two trumpet players.
George Kelly?
No, no, George played the tenor saxophone.
Guy Kelly. from New Orleans.
Guy Kelly. And they were with a show named Gonzell White. This was the first time that I ever saw a hundred dollar bill. Gonzell White had it. That was Basie's
Basie was traveling with that show?
Road show.
Yeah, before he...
Gonzell White. Now those two names may not be the other two musicians that were with him, but there were two trumpet players and Basie. That was when I first met Basie. That was back in 1925 or 1926.
Before he even came to Kansas City.
Yeah, yeah. Now, let's see. Abe Bowler , you know, the bass player. Abe was in Kansas City. 'Cause Abe was with the Blue Devils too, you know. And...
You worked with Bunk Johnson in Kansas City...

Let me tell you, Ellis Burden asked me who we could get from New Orleans, you know, that...just to have around because... the music wasn't important, you see. He had a gambling house. See..these...it's just like a gambling house...and having the music, that's just a come-on for people to come, and the man to bring his lady, and she'll listen to the music and he'll go back and gamble. Same way as we talked about a record...making records...having a record store. Well, you get your shoes shined and you hear a record and you buy it. So that's the way that was.
Let's see now...what did I say...
Why did he want to get somebody from New Orleans?
Well, as an attraction, you know. People, you know... well, Sammy Price from Texas, slick dude, you know, smart and you know, know a lot of people, he's popular. You know,

because people come in, buy drinks and gamble and all that, and so he said...I suggested that we get Bunk Johnson. Well, we got Bunk Johnson and by the time that he got there he was so darn high that he didn't know where he was. I don't think Bunk even remembered even coming to Kansas City. 'Cause he stayed around there two or three days and we couldn't do anything with him at all. So we sent him back to New Orleans. He tried to play, but he couldn't play. And lost his cap and you know and all that business. But he couldn't play. He came to Kansas City with the intention of playing, but he didn't quite accomplish his mission.
Had you heard of him?

I'd heard of him, yeah, because see, back when I was coming through that period of Charleston and all that, there was a New Orleans band that came from New Orleans with Professor Sherman Cook. Professor Sherman Cook, Lee Collins, a little boy named LeRoy...I can't think of LeRoy's last name. Percy Darensbourg, Caffrey Darensbourg, Freddie Bobo and a fellow named Octave playing the piano.

I'll tell you about this band from New Orleans. I could only play 'My Isle of Golden Dreams,' or a few songs, or if you start a song off, you know, I could probably come in. So this band--Son Lewis and Cal Liston, who had a dance hall they called it the Skunk...well, they called it...what the hell, some dance hall in Dallas. And they used to like go to other towns and have dances two or three days a week.

So then they said...they needed a piano player. And the piano player, Octave, got high and got homesick for some of that gum-bo and, you know, just...You know, and those fellows couldn't contain themselves. They just went like insane, you know, not to do anything harmful, but just longing for home, you know? So this guy went home. And they said, "Well, we've got to have a piano player to play the dance," so they picked me. And I said to them, "Now look, I'm no piano player when it come down to this business. But if you start a song off, you know like if we're playing 'Sheik' and you stomp it off, da-da-da, when you play the first few notes then I can come in. But don't depend on me to come in and leading it."

That was agreeable, Dan. And then when we got to Mineral Wells, or Wichita Falls or wherever the hell it was, everything changed. They'd bring the music; "Now, in the fourteenth bar you will do this and do that." Now we discover that the piano is not in tune. So in order for them to play in B-flat, I would have to play in B-natural. Well, I couldn't play in B-flat too well to begin with. Now, if they're puttin' me in B-natural, I'm really in trouble. So, this night these guys start a song. I couldn't come in because I'd have to play in B-natural. If I played the chords, if I knew them, I'd be playing in the wrong key.
So they did that to me for two or three days. And I told them, "Now," you know what I mean, "Let's cool it." But what they would always do, Dan, and I guess this is typical of any

person that..where there are two or three people can speak a different language from one person, they'll speak in that language and say something and even if they're not talking about the person, he will think they're talking about him. They used to speak this patois, so coming back from Mineral Wells or wherever it was--we were in this big Cadillac, we had all the instruments and all this business--and they kept talking that patois and I was in the back and I came out with a gun and fired and you're talking about Frenchmen leaving--you ever see rats leave a ship--I ran 'em all down the highway and wouldn't let them come back to the car, and the guy that was the manager, they were coming in a car behind us and they saw all these Frenchmen all around.."b'uhbluhbluhbluhbluh," you know, it killed me (laughter). So finally, Cal Liston say, "Put that gun away," you know what I mean. So I got in the car with the manager and then I went back to Dallas. They never forgot that incident out on the highway, but...because... and the guy drivin' the car, we called him Trembling Slim. He said, "I told you all don't mess with Sam Price, that's one of the Price Boys." (Laughter).

But we got in Chicago and I went around every morning to the breakfast dance. You see, they had a breakfast dance. This is a thing they had every morning. They used to have those here. They called it a breakfast dance, it's just where they had a special show...say at four o'clock, the place closed at four or five o'clock. They'd have music and a dance

and all of the people...I guess it was one way that each club would have of increasing its business and, you know, people who wouldn't have an opportunity to go could go. So, they had breakfast dances every morning at one of the different clubs. And I never will forget, on Sunday night it was at the Club De-Lisa that would have...that's where Albert Ammons was playing, you know. And they had a big show and all that, and they'd have this big breakfast dance and hundreds of people, you know, come and try to get in, you know, and people from other clubs and people from the Panama. This is where King Cole used to play. And people from the DeLuxe. And Jimmie Noone's band, and Teddy Wilson's band, and musicians that played out on the north side, you know what I mean, the white spots. And downtown. They would all come to these various breakfast dances.

And I never will forget one morning, they had a breakfast dance at 49th and South Parkway.// Earl Hines came in with a party and I jumped up from my table and ran over to the piano and started playing "Deep Forest." That's his theme song. And the people thought I was crazy, you know. "Man, don't you see Earl Hines"? and "What are you trying to play his song...," you know. I only wanted to let Earl Hines know that I loved him so, that I knew his song. But the guys made it look like that I was crazy. So I had to sneak out the back door, you know what I mean. And I had them...I played them in four concerts--Denison, Greenville, Dallas and Paris, Texas. Very, very successful. So it's that funny feeling that you get, Dan, during...you promote something that you believe in and that you find out that other people...you convince them, too.

But in New York City guys wondered for years how I was making it, and I had a very simple pattern. Especially with blacks, because some places were kind of funny, you know...sit you behind posts and all that shit...

Behind the post? Well, not really, and in one sense, yes. But I can't pinpoint it. Like Leon and

And even the Theresa. You couldn't get a room in the Theresa, you know what I mean, during some period back there. So Billy Rose wasn't at the Diamond Horseshoe. They asked me to come over to his house on Sutton Place. So I went over to Billy's house and we became like father and son, or brother...two brothers. So he says, "Sam, now I'll tell you. I don't care what happens, you got the job." He wanted two piano players. "You got one of the jobs. Don't worry." Now, we rehearsed this show; we tried out in Detroit; we played Philadelphia; and one day in New York when we were getting ready to open, Tallulah Bankhead went up on the right side of the theater and there was a scene where that you could not see her, you know, for that's like a fleeting moment. She would disappear from view. And she said to Billy, and God for me to give me if they don't want tell what happened. She said to Billy, "Billy, I'm lost." And then she recited lines, "And you will go in a daddledede-dat." Then she's back in view. Do you know that she told him to change that and he wouldn't. And she barred him from the theater. She wouldn't let him come in the theater. She said, "If you come in here, I'm not doing the show." And he had to stay away, so the show finally closed. It later became a very successful movie, but they didn't carry out the idea about the music, I don't think. I don't...
As far as I remember, no.
Because that whole thing was just "Freight Train Blues," you know, that kind of, you know what I mean, you know,

triplets, you know, thirds, and, you know what I mean, things like that, and tremolo. But the show closed, and it later became a movie, but I don't think that that movie carried the theme which would have been, you know...maybe they perhaps could have used a clarinet to play, you know what I mean crescendoes and all that business.

But the show closed, and after that I went to 52nd Street, and I went back to the Café Society. And then we opened a place in Brooklyn and I had the band out there with Max the Mayor. So I showed them... 'Hey Max, how many bottles of whiskey you got? Twenty? Okay. How many you putting out on the bar? Twenty. Okay, put out ten. Put ten in reserve, then check on the bottles, see what's left and, you know, estimate what the remaining amount of whiskey's left in the bottle. How many cans of...' They'd just have a whole lot of cans of beer or bottles of beer, and just have it stacked up with a whole lot of iced soda and sell it and, you know, half the bottles gone and they don't know from nothing. Plus I had the band.

Now in exchange for me doing that, what I did for him to help him, he gave me the band and he let me have the checkroom. Well, I was always all right with...these people were supposed to be underworld people, or gangsters, or whatever they were...I didn't know. But I always...I could get checkrooms. You know, so this is how I'm making a living.

God, I don't know how I'm making a living. And I knew everybody. Because of the fact that many of these people who I knew in the territories (and) in the various cities, if they were not living in New York, they'd come here. And when they'd come here they'd look me up. So guys just could not figure that out. So that's how I survived over the years. That's how I survived.
