Bernie. That's right.
They were so filthy rich it wasn't even funny. One of them was the District Attorney, wasn't he?
Something like that, yeah.

So, that's how I made it in New York City. And plus the fact that I usually try to help people. Then you know, you remember Adam Clayton Powell. The first political advisor he had was my uncle and this is how I happened to go into the political arena. I had a license on Broadway as a booking agent. Legitimate booking agent. Not, you know, sub-booking for somebody or, you know, I'm waiting for it to be approved.
I had an office at 1674 Broadway. That's where I gave Willie 'the Lion' and James P. Johnson an office just to come and play...

Adam Clayton Powell...this was during the early days before he, you know, went into politics proper...There was a man in central Harlem named Joseph E. Ford. Joe Ford was my uncle. And, aside from having all these other good things happen to me, you know, getting jobs and making records and broadening my acquaintance with a lot of people...then when I find Uncle Joe, I find him in an NAACP boat ride I believe it was. They were giving an NAACP boat ride. And this man was standing down at 125th Street on the pier, selling tickets for this boat ride. And I had eight people with me, and I walked up to him and I recognized him. I hadn't seen him...this was 1937 and I hadn't seen him since 1913. And he was saying, "tickets?" And I said, "Yes, I want eight tickets." And I said, "I've been looking for you." And I guess he thought I was the FBI or something. So he said, "What did I do now?" I says, "Do you know who I am?" He says, "No. How many tickets do you want?" I says, "I'm your sister's son."

Now, he had not heard from us from 1913 to 1937...'38. I said, "I am your sister's son." And he was a dark man. He turned snow white for a moment. And he was flabbergasted when he found out who I was and that it was real. It took me a moment to say, "Well now your father's name was Albert and your mother's name was Mary Jane. And then I started naming his sisters...you know, flashbacks, to acquaint him with, you
know, who was what and what. So then we had a big reunion and on the boat, and then I met Adam Powell. And this was my introduction to the political arena.

He managed Adam's political affairs and he was also District Leader and he was in the Borough President's office, and he was a kingmaker, of course. He never sought any political office, but people running for office always tried to get his support in order to, you know, function and to be successful. And he helped to elect Roosevelt.../this was about the time/ well, the last time we re-elected Roosevelt and then he died. And Roosevelt died at the time that my uncle had helped me get this booking agency license. And I was on Broadway still working for Decca and I had been approached by James P. Johnson's people to help with the "Yamacraw" concert that they were having in Carnegie Hall.

But the problem that they were having, they didn't have enough money to write the score and in some way I was involved in helping to get that score prepared, and helping them to present "Yamacraw" in Carnegie Hall. But the tragedy of the thing was that the day that we were having the concert, was the date that Roosevelt died, and the date that Roosevelt died, the world stood still. So it meant that we had to have an adjournment; we had to postpone the thing for a week and the enthusiasm wasn't there as it was for the first thing. As a result, I don't know...I don't think I made a profit. I didn't care. I didn't want to make a profit 'cause, I told you, I
never liked to profiteer off of musicians. I don't, you know... if I take something out from a musician, I'll put it back.
And then James P. and I became very close because he knew that I was, you know, proud of him as a man and an artist, and he was very grateful to me for that until his death.
It was unfortunate that he never had much luck with his, you know, with his major works on this...

Well, I think he didn't have the success with them because people...Broadway...the promoters forgot that here's a man that wrote a song, 'The Charleston,' that should have endeared him to the entire world, and that anything that he wanted to do, he should have been able to find support.

For example, Dan, I'm in a peculiar position now. I've always been interested in trying to stimulate local interest in activities like Jazz Festival Society in Chicago---in Philadelphia, and I organized the New York Jazz Festival Society here. I haven't done anything important with it. But I think that, why can't mainstreams and guys who know the history of jazz, why can't we begin to build in black communities this kind of thing where incubators are created and out of that can evolve more of the original kind of things that's needed."
But sometimes I blame writers, you know what I mean, guys--I'm not calling any names 'cause they know who they are--who would create a term like Be-bop, Swing, Jazz, Honky-tonk, etc., etc., etc. All of these came out of a certain basic pattern. And no matter be it Charlie Parker...I played a concert with
Charlie Parker and he said to me, 'Sam, you just play what you play and I'll play what I play and it'll come out all right.'

So, at 71, having played the piano 58 years, you know what I mean, I feel like that I have something to say or something to contribute, and that it should be put down and it should not be...the fact that I played for thirty years and for ten years nobody heard of me. That's what happened with Bunk Johnson...that's a cardinal example. They didn't hear from him 'cause he didn't have any teeth. They didn't hear from him because he was on a rice field.

Where was the lineage? Where was the direct line so that you could see, Dan...where...what happened in 1908, '09, '10, '11, '12, '13, '14, '15 should not be a break in the history of blacks in jazz. I say this, and I say it quite candidly, that I've been very, very disturbed that Duke Ellington died several years ago...do they play his music? Yes. And I'm sure they get the royalties. I'm sure that he was astute enough to have that kind of arrangement, and lawyers and...to take care of that. But what about heritage? What about the roots? What about the tradition? What about the carrying it on? What about...do you see? What about his son living in Denmark, I'm told, and, /he inherited the band. Where's the band? Where's the incubator? Where are the new creators coming out of Duke's idiom? Where are the creators coming out of Louis Armstrong?
I took Johnny Letman on a tour in Europe a few days ago...and incidentally, I want to talk to you about Europe, too,

I want to tell you some of the things...good things that I think have happened. Two years ago I took Johnny Letman on a tour for Honestier, and we had Ronnie Cole on the drums, we had George Kelly, we had Bill Pemberton, and I played the piano,and Fred Alonzo the trombone player, a young man from New Orleans...a good trombone player that's one of the few trombone...promising trombone players that I've heard from Louisiana. I've heard him in Bern, Switzerland, year before last with Wally Davenport. I heard him in that band. He's quite...you know what I mean...he's young but he is steeped in the tradition of jazz and sliding and glissing and, you know what I mean, and growling and mutes, and etcetera.

Now, I took Johnny Letman to Europe, '77, I think it was. We played...we were in Yugoslavia...we played Zagreb and Belgrade. We were in Portugal, Caïscas, played Paris...all over. All right? The highlight of that tour was when I introduced Johnny Letman and said, and I said it like this, "Ladies and Gentlemen, I would like to present a young man from America, steeped in the tradition of Louis Armstrong. Louis Armstrong has gone, and will not return, so I'm going to ask each of you here in this room to close your eyes and sit down and reminisce as Johnny Letman plays 'Sleepy Time Down South.'" It was fantastic. In Portugal, in Cosh Cosh, he did "Hello Dolly" and "Sleepy Time Down South" and we got a five-minute standing ovation. Five minutes. That happened to me once before in Madrid... in Barcelona. I played for people there in 1956 and when these
people stood up so long I thought I'd done something wrong. I said, 'What the hell did I do wrong'? They said, 'You're a big hit.'

So the idea is that we must begin now, and say now, and I'm willing to be one of the creators...I've...incidentally, I've just been named as one of the members of the board of a cultural thing that we're doing here in central Harlem... they're going to spend seventy or eighty million dollars on this project and I'm on the Board of Directors. And I most certainly intend to see...and what actually happened was that Assemblyman George W. Miller called a meeting to report on this affair and the board members consisted of Harry Belafonte and Ossie Davis and great guys who've already made it. But I got up and I said to them, 'You have got to have some of the present day people who are here on the scene to have some input in this thing. Because you can't tell me that you can have a garage two blocks away from a center and not determine how the people are going to get from that garage to the center and from the center back to the garage. It's the same as with the subway, and whatever idea that you adopt can be...probably be the idea that you can use to create a better tone in central Harlem, or in Harlem, whereby that blacks can become more interested in jazz.'

And my feelings are that we are going to have to join together and to be motivated and to do some of these things just as the...you take Billy Taylor. Billy Taylor has done one hell of a job for modern jazz. He's been in on all of the committees,

you know what I mean, he's been where the, you know, where the money's allocated and appropriated and where the plans are formulated...he's been in on all of that. So as a result of that, his Jazzmobile has been a success.

You have very few older musicians playing on the darn thing, so I think that simultaneously with that...I don't say to cut it out...I say but add more to another facet so that you've got maybe thirty concerts underwritten by the city with the union and thirty different public places, where the jazz musicians can come...the best can come and play and be presented and to make the world aware that a lot of these great guys...like Procope. He's still living and playing very well. But you don't hear anything about it. You've got George Kelly... even Sonny Greer, as feeble as he...he's getting old, but then, he's here. The people should see him. They should know who he is. Here's Jo Jones, one of the greatest percussionists of all time. He's here. Here's Doc Cheatham, who is doing the best that he can, you know, but he should have the right kind of support so that he don't have to...when he go on a job... wonder who's playing drums or wonder...because the impresario will pick the band.

And I think that we should build more bands. We should bring Eddie Heywood back down here. I understand he's been ailing, but we should bring him back and let them see the guy that wrote "Canadian Sunset." Let him see the guy that made the arrangement on "Begin the Beguine." These are the things
that I think that need to happen, Dan, and we're going to be remiss in our duty if we don't do something about these things. Now you wanted to ask me something about how I made it in Texas...
I wanted to ask you about growing up in Texas a long time ago. Was it difficult to survive?

Well, as a child, it was not more difficult for me than for it was/my parents. My parents were the ones that had...my father...he was the mayor, the black mayor. He was in the most danger. Because if a black kid did something in Texas, they'd just send him away to a reform school and they'd keep him 'til he's 21. And that's the end of that and a lot of kids knew it. So, sometimes when a black kid became involved in some wrongdoing, he just went the limit, 'cause he know what to expect anyway. The least he could expect is the electric chair. Sometimes kids are just immune to that. They're just immune to death; they're immune to pain, you know what I mean, and... But it was dangerous in a sense. You had to be...had certain places you couldn't go. Those were very, very stringent restrictions. In any place that there were white people and "Thank you, Missy," you had to take your hat off and, "Yessir, no sir,"/and "Please" and you had to be very, very humble, and you had to be aware... Of course, what I did when I was 14 or 15, I did away with a hat. I figured there was no point in having to tip my hat or take my hat off to anybody so I just threw the damn thing away. That eliminated part of that problem. Although from time to

time since then I've worn hats, but it wasn't under the conditions where that I had to be, you know, be humble with my hat. And I'm courteous anyway. I probably would just tip my hat to a person and take my hat off as a matter of courtesy, because I feel within that that's the feeling that a person should have.

But a black kid knew that he'd go to the reform school... and it was called Gatesville, in Texas, and they, you know what I mean...the stories that used to come out of Gatesville were stories of brutality that you never heard of. And so it was very, very dangerous in a sense. Couldn't be out late at night...parents, you know, like to know where you are...and they would arrest them and...a thousand and one things. So it was dangerous, but if you were wise, if you were smart, and you were not negligent, you could survive. That's the way that was. But...
Later on, being on the road, like the TOBA and so on, were there problems?

Yeah, you'd have problems. For example, in Atlanta they had two shows at night and then on Friday night they'd have a midnight show. Now, you were not supposed to be on the street after 12 o'clock if you were black in Atlanta. Now, if you forgot to get your letter or your pass from the man that owned the 81 Theater stating that I'm just going home from work, I just did a show, they put you in jail and hold you overnight.

Sometimes they'd put a guy in jail and he'd be wanted for something else someplace else, so you had be be very careful. I've known many nights that guys would stay in the theater all night. They'd stay in the dressing room...sleep in the theater all night.

In Pensacola, Florida, if you went on the stage and didnt't have pantyhose...opera lengths, they called them...that stocking, you know, that...they'd put you in jail for that. And if you got in jail in Pensacola, they put you in jail in Pensacola, they'd let you out to do the show. Then you'd have to go back in jail. Like if a guy get three days in jail, you know, for doing something, he could...they'd let him come out and do the show and then he'd spend the rest of the time in jail. And in Florida they didn't allow you on the beach without a pass, you had to have a written pass.

And you couple that with most of those states...you had to have, in order to participate in the political activities, you had to have...what did they call that voter's thing?...you had to have a poll tax receipt. But now the funny thing, that with all of these laws, there always was some white man that could call up the police and get you out of jail.

I remember, in my home, I used to ride a motorcycle. I learned how to ride a motorcycle out at the fair ground. At the fair park each year they had...at the Dallas Fair...you know what I mean, they had this big carnival. You know, and fairs. and Ferris wheels and cotton candy and shows, and I used to hang around the Motor
Drome. That's where the people they had there used to ride the motorcycles. The thing would stay there all summer.

Well, naturally, the people knew me. They let me start up the motorcycles and warm them up because, you know, they wouldn't want to go on the Motor Drome with a cold bike...cold motor. So that I could start the motor up and I'd sit on it, you know, I thought I was a big shot. I'd sit on the motorcycle, you know, and race the motor and keep it warmed up, and then when the guy's ready to go ride, I just, you know, just pushed it off the rack and he'd go on up.

So one day this guy pushed the motorcycle off of that stand and the lady asked me to just ride around the bottom part on the ground...you know, on the floor part. So I was just riding around very slow... she said, "Keep the motor warm." So finally she said, "Go up just a little bit on that thing." So I went up just a little. And she say, "Go up a little higher, now." And what happened, Danny, when she told me to go up a little higher, I went up a little higher, and she was on the motorcycle, right? All right, she got between me and the floor and that made me have to go up on the damn thing. Well, I knew the principle of a motor pulling, in order that you won't fall...gravity...if you keep the motor pulling it pulls against the gravity...but I mean the gravity is pulling against the motor, so it's a question of who win.

So I'm riding like hell, up, and she's down below. And her husband get on the motorcycle and shoot up above me. Now, here I am, riding // that was the most frightening motorcycle ride I have ever had.

How did it wind up?

I know that I became a feature with the...with this Motor Drome, and they used to let me ride. That was one of the feature things...one of the feature acts, because they had a black kid riding this motorcycle...looked like a ham sandwich and I'd always be in the middle of...I'd go up just like I did...I had enough nerve to go up...and I'd go up...I never went up higher than the middle of that ring, that dome, you know. So I stayed around with them all the summer. I was getting, you know, that traveling blood and all that. I did so many different things when I was young.

One of the things I used to do...in Dallas they had a thing called...they had two jails, the city jail and the county jail. If you were in the city jail, arrested for something, and they transferred you to the county jail, after they filed charges against you...well, they had a thing called a writ of habeas corpus. The lawyer would get this and the judge would

sign it. But I don't exactly remember how I...whether I used to swipe them from the lawyer...but anyway, I'd get the kid's name, you understand, and then I'd put it on that thing and then take it to a judge...this one judge who knew when I first used to take them for a lawyer . Then I'd take them to this judge and he'd always sign it. And I got a lot of black kids out of jail that way. And they never did catch on to it. I guess if they'd caught on to it I'd have really went to Gatesville. I was about 15. That was just one of the many things I used to do extracurricular. (Laughter).

You know, speaking of going to Europe and of my trip to Europe that time, when I accidentally went over in 1948 instead of Willie, I made a lot of friends. I made friends with Panassié, Charles Delaunay, Curt Moore , Jack Dimitri. I met was not on the scene, this guy who...Jack Morgantini. Those days Monestier / the one who had the Hot Clubs promoting concerts and you had to make contacts with him.

In Philadelphia he played at the Academy of Music and when we became good friends sometimes I would stay in Philadelphia and he would meet the musicians at the station, here in New York, at Penn Station, with the tickets. And, you know what I mean, sort of act like a group leader, and bring them over.
So now Mezz and I became friends and he reciprocated--he found an angel who had money and he let me make those records

that /I made with Cousin Joe and Socks Wilson, and Coot Grant and Hot Lips Page, and then I made a series of things, "Step Down, Step Up," and "133" and all that. He reciprocated. And then in '48 when we went to the festival and Willie 'the Lion' didn't go, I went with him. So we became very, very close. But, as I said, those guys always would, in the end, not try to do anything to you, but try to make you make mistakes. And so, for that reason...but we never fell out.

Now, in 1956 I was in Paris, and Mezz had an opportunity to...I invited him to this...the Consul General in Paris invited me...Sammy Price there, with the band, playing for the Jeunesse Musical...one of the, you know...so I'm up in the upper strata. And Mezz didn't want me to go.

Now his reason...I do not know why he didn't...the Arthurine Lucy case; it was in Topeka, or wherever it was, and they were having problems. You know, we were in the height of decisions being made that have to do with race. And Mezz just felt like that I should not have gone to the Embassy. And I told him, I said, "Well, one thing had nothing to do with the other. I think that it's an honor for me, if the American Government invited me to come to the American Embassy and, hell... I'm going. And the only reason that I don't go is that I have a stroke, or die before. But when my government respect me enough, and honor me with a visit to them, then they're sure that I'm carrying some kind of prestige."

So Sidney came, and then he and Sidney got into a big fight about it because Sidney felt that I should have gone, too. So...but that was the only difficult time that we had other than the royalties. And we always would end up on that.
What about plans.. People had divided opinions about Mezzrow as a musician.

I think that a lot of people, because of the fact that Mezz was so anxious to...I think he was one white man that wanted to be colored, you know? That's very simple. I can understand it. He wanted to be colored. All right, he wanted to be colored but he wasn't. He was a white man. He was in...he married a black woman, you understand, and he had kids by this black woman and, you know. But he just wasn't a black man. But if he could have been a black man, he would have been one. And when a person is thinking a certain way, you gotta be careful that people don't misunderstand. You know he's just sitting there 'cause he's a white man trying to be nice to folks. But that's really not the way it is. So I say that he just couldn't be colored, just couldn't be that. If there was any such/him being thing as it I'm sure he'd have been it. But he proved that he was faithful and...but he just couldn't be one...a colored person. And I believe that he wanted to be.
He said that in his book. (Really the Blues)
What...
That that is what he wanted...
But he's just talking through his hat. I told him

quite frankly, not to insult him, I said, "Mezz, I'm what you want to be. I'm a black man. You want to be one. But There ain't a damn thing you can do to make yourself be one, but be born again." But he was a nice guy...he was, you know...a lot of people misunderstood him. He'd talk a lot...
Oh, yeah.
He's talk beyond his fondest dream.
He could play for a long time...

Beyond his fondest dream. Some guy walks in with him to Jimmy Ryan's one night and says, "You know what?" Says, "Milton Mezzrow's the only guy I know could make a clarinet sound like it's got hay fever. (Laughter).

I once heard, before the days of long solos, you know... before Coltrane, in the forties, , I think he was playing "Black and Blue." And he played...I'd never heard anybody play that long before, you know...fifteen minutes.
"Black and Blue" became red and pink...(laughter). But he was a good old...good old boy from Chicago. He was a good old boy.
In the '20s, and even in the early '30swas there much contact between black and white musicians?

It was select and rare.Like, a white guy get a chance to play with some black musicians, he was happy as hell. Cop catch you around in a black neighborhood and beat the hell out of him. Make 'em get on away from there. Some white boys were more daring than others. Some white boys didn't give a damn. They'd take a whippin'.........Shit......... I remember
in Dallas when I was there, take '54...as late as '54, this white guy came up playing in a club. Cop beat the hell out of him.
That late?
Yeah, '54.

There's some rare...some isolated cases. They find out that you're all right. For example, like they found out I was all right. Right there in Dallas fifty years worked at the Elks Club, you know, white club, so they would give me a break more so than they would some other guy that they didn't like. Because they had Jim Crow laws and they could enforce it if (inaudible) they wanted to. And many of them did. But as a whole, I think that I was fortunate, to get through all this and ..end up telling some of it on paper. Talking about it.

Talking about box suppers, you know what I mean, and church on Saturdays and prayer meeting on Friday night, church services on Sunday, and going to hear gospel singing and going to hear Church of God singing, and hearing the singers with the triangles and tambourines, you know what I mean, and those broken down organs and then, from that, going to picnics where, you know, there'd be two or three thousand people...the picnic grounds, and going fishing and then we would do all these things... and having lived through two world wars and one Korean conflict, and having lived through [the] epidemic in 1918, where that there were hundreds of thousands of people wiped out during the smallpox...and having lived in the Jim Crow South where that your life wasn't worth a damn if you were black, you know what I mean.

And having lived through all of that, and having left Dallas and went on up and down that road show, and learned that fidelity, and learned that training ground, and come back...and going to Kansas City, and going to Chicago, and going to Detroit. Then coming to New York. And from New York stretching out across the sea. Going to Europe and meeting Panassié and authorities and cardinals and vice president and president .

And having had the opportunitcy to meet people in the record industry like Al Jolson and Jack Kapp, and Bing Crosby and Ella Fitzgerald and black, great musicians like Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington. And meeting Guy Lombardo and meeting...you name it and I've met them. From Hubert Humphrey on down to Danny Morgenstern. To do all of these things in 71 years, and to start from that humble beginning where my grandmother had them put a big pot in the back yard, three bricks high, five stacks, fill it full of hot water, and to be born. And to come through all of that with a midwife...and a grandmother was a midwife...to come through all of that and to come out of the bowels of the ghetto into the mainstream of American life. I say, Dan, that I made a lot of money, and spent every penny. I spent every penny.

Yesterday I sat here with you, and when I sat here with you yesterday I had a thousand dollars in my pocket. Today I have twenty-two dollars. This is the way...you heard my daughter ask me for a fur coat you know, yesterday. I'll give it

to her. People ask me for things, I give them. I don't have any value on money as, like Fort Knox. People say to me, " The dollars there," and so what. I don't want... All I do, I go, when a man want me to go to Europe and play for him and appear; he set his conditions out; I tell him what I want in dollars; he send me a plane ticket, or if he don't I buy my own ticket and go; meet him there. Have me a comfortable room, warm, with a bath and show, you know what I mean, and it's clean, and food. And he has no trouble out of... I don't have to have no Rémy-Martin or Tom, Dick and Harry, or... I gotta have me two highballs before I play my first song.

Now my life is patterned like that. It's very simple. But I'm glad it is because I've been able to survive. If I had to have like three packages of cigarettes a day, must be Kools, and a drink of Scotch on the rocks, plenty of ice and, you know, and all that, I couldn't survive. Because what would happen if you didn't have it? When I don't have... when I'm not, you know, in shape, I can stay at home. Dan, I'm home at 8 o'clock at night, looking out the window. Variety. All of this here didn't just get on those pages, plus other things that... you know, I just didn't bring any of those things out. I didn't want to bring them. I got two hundred pictures. I'm getting ready to label my pictures that's going to go in the book
But I say that what I am more concerned with than anything is why can't the black musicians rally together. Just
for their own salvation. Just for the sake of the art form being preserved. Am I sounding too unreal? What do you think?
No. It would be a logical thing to do. It seems hard to get musicians to organize to work together on something like that.

Yep.

Yeah...

But let her do the whole concert behind the shim, you know, and Billie Holiday's silhouette, with the trumpet player playing, and then, let her come out, and them lights so dim you can't see her, and when she say, "Gloomy SUN...day," then the lights come on bright.

Those guys, they don't have--how to measure anything. They have no measurement of concept. That's why they match up musicians in the (unintelligible). It's a simple thing...

Because what it's done...it has killed band leaders. They don't have any organized small groups. Years ago you had the Savoy Saltons, Louis Jordan's Tympany Five, you know... you name it and you had a group. But today you don't have any of that.
All you have is All Stars...
Sammy Price and Friends. So some guy says, 'Sammy Price is playing with some of his friends, and some of them are his enemies. (Laughter).

So Dan, I'm...I'm...I hope that people will get some little, you know, interest out of the knowledge of the things that I've pointed out. I haven't said anything with malice. I've said some things that a guy may not like, but it wasn't intentional. And if I said it intentionally and he didn't like it, I don't care. You know, I don't care. Because I know I've treated everybody all right. Guys say, 'You know, when first met you I didn't like you. Now that I know you, I hate
you. (Laughter). But I think that I've tried to give you some of the things that, you know, that perhaps have helped you on your way...

No, I think that you (unintelligible)...One thing that, you know, we're trying to do is to get things from musicians which you too often have to sift/ed through somebody else's, you know, and not get it straight.

Right.
And Velma Middleton? Jack Teagarden?
Yeah, we got that whole band. ...
But there's one guy that we left out that was a good man. You know who that was?
Pop Wilson.
Right. (Laughter).
Well, he was just a kid then anyway.
Well, he played pretty good, though.
That thing that I did with Milt Hinton was called "Barrelhouse Blues and Boogie Woogie." That was the name of that album. With Vic Dickenson, Cozy Cole, Pete Brown and Jonah Jones.
Did I tell you I did that Langston Hughes story, Tambourines to Glory?
Yes.
It was a gospel thing with Hazel Scott and Clara Ward,
Nipsy Russell...
That was quite successful...

No..mhm mhm. I had begged Langston...this was the forerunner of the Eubie and Don't Bother Me and all of that. I told Langston, "Langston, don't make this a play. Make it a musical." But I don't know if he had the say so, or if he was, you know, who had the rights to the book. But if they'd of made that a musical it would still be running. It would still been running. Because it was a good book.
I don't know if I told you about the Crawdaddy test .
No, no, you didn't tell me about that.

The Crawdaddy, you know, that was just a place with 35 people eating in a room and Musak. It was formerly the room where Guy Lombardo played and I went in there, and inside of one year they would bring one hundred and seventy-five dinners... Eubie Blake...they had a big birthday party...they had a big celebration there and Eubie Blake crowned me King of Boogie-Woogie. He said...when he came in, he says, "Sammy," and he put the crown on my head, "I crown you King of Boogie-Woogie. But I don't kiss men." (Laughter). And then we had a big festival outside. But right after that I went to the Gstaad to the Chess ey Club. That's the ski area. You haven't been to Gstaad. That's G S T A A D. And Jay McShann played there, Carrie Smith and a lot of people...gospel singers. Played the Popcorn Club, of course. I did more business...you know, I set a few records around, you know. I think the people...a lot

of lay persons knew me. But the guy that's the operator would be listening to modern musicians some and you know, and didn't hire me, but I would come, and they would think...because the man that owned that Popcorn Club said that I was the only one that at 2 o'clock, when the place was closing, the place was still packed and they were demanding encores. And those were his exact words.

I had a really really strange experience with Big Mama Thornton down at the Cookery. You know, she made "You Ain't Nothin' But a Houn' Dog," and she was really a strange person. But she knew...she knew the blues, you know.
I played that piano summit out at Waterloo Village last year.
Right.
That was something, man. Had all these fine piano players and I washed them away. One big broom and a bucket of water.
No gas...
'No,' (laughter) "No Gas Boogie." Who told you about that?
Oh, I heard it long ago...

But George Wein, you know, I was fighting with Menestier and he didn't want to get into it, you know, and he just stayed out of it. I give George credit for that. You know George always...never (unintelligible)..."Hey, you gotta work that out with Sam."

One of these days I'm going to check up to see how many... I'm going to check all the records I made and see how many times I made the same song over again, just to see which one is in the lead...whether it's "St. James Infirmary," or "Sweet Georgia Brown"...
"Honeysuckle Rose"...
Or "Honeysuckle Rose." Well, what do you think now?
I think we've got it.

And we're bringing people to Harlem. Taking them around and showing them Harlem. We won't do that, Dan. Person want a picture, we will have a friendly rapport with people that he can make a

picture with. And all in all I predict a bright future for jazz. I think I'm going to...what I want to try to do is work very closely with that boy...what's his name? From the school that play the bass?

Yeah, he is on a committee at the National Endowment for the Arts...Music in Schools. And...

own code and you can't tell how long a thing's been up there.

But, do you need me for any additional...

I don't think so. So I think we're all right. But I know that if I do, I can always, you know, get in touch with you and ask you...but I think this will...We covered a lot of ground, as you say, you know, from Honey Grove and...
From that big 'pot'. (Laughter). Well, all right, so if there's nothing else...
